qs.q: A 50-year-old woman with chronic alcohol use disorder is admitted and experiences acute alcohol withdrawal with tremors and agitation. Why is diazepam effective in managing this condition?
o: It acts as a primary analgesic to relieve somatic pain
It directly blocks NMDA receptors to prevent seizures
It enhances GABA-mediated inhibition to calm excitability
It stimulates dopamine release in the mesolimbic pathway
qs.e: Abrupt alcohol withdrawal causes increased CNS excitability due to altered signalling; diazepam enhances GABA-mediated inhibition to control these symptoms. Diazepam does not act as a primary analgesic.

qs.q: A 48-year-old woman is admitted to the ward with severe alcohol withdrawal symptoms, including tremors, sweating, and perceptual disturbances. Why is diazepam a preferred agent in this clinical scenario?
o: Functions as an SSRI to balance mood fluctuations
Directly activates aldehyde dehydrogenase, lowering acetaldehyde levels
Speeds up liver enzymes that clear remaining ethanol
Offers cross‑tolerance and reduces CNS over‑activity by enhancing GABA‑A
qs.e: Diazepam is a major use in alcohol withdrawal because it shares cross-tolerance and enhances GABA inhibition to counter CNS hyperexcitability. It does not affect aldehyde dehydrogenase or act as an SSRI.

qs.q: Which of the following is a common symptom associated with alcohol withdrawal syndrome?
qs.e: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome results from the central nervous system's adaptation to chronic alcohol exposure. Symptoms often include tremors, anxiety, hallucinations, tachycardia, hypertension, and potentially life-threatening seizures and delirium tremens.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Alcohol withdrawal is a neuro‑chemical rebound after chronic alcohol use, presenting with autonomic hyperactivity, anxiety, tremor and seizures. Prompt recognition and benzodiazepine therapy prevents fatal complications.

sections.p: Alcohol withdrawal occurs when a person with chronic alcohol dependence stops or reduces intake. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by the CIWA‑Ar score and history of heavy drinking.

t.b: Assesses withdrawal severity; higher scores mean more severe autonomic and neuro symptoms, guiding benzodiazepine dosing

sections.p: Severity is staged by CIWA‑Ar: mild (0‑7), moderate (8‑15), severe (16‑24), life‑threatening (>24).

t.b: Determines need for benzodiazepines and monitoring intensity

sections.p: Primary cause is chronic alcohol consumption leading to GABA‑A receptor down‑regulation and glutamate up‑regulation. In low‑resource settings, co‑infections (HIV, TB, malaria) and malnutrition worsen withdrawal.

t.b: Detects hypokalemia, which can precipitate seizures

sections.p: Early signs: anxiety, tremor, nausea. Progression: autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension), hallucinations, seizures, delirium tremens.
Basic labs guide safety and identify complications. In low‑resource settings, focus on electrolytes, liver function, and infection markers.

t.b: Low levels increase seizure risk; replace if <3.5 mmol/L
Elevated AST/ALT suggest hepatic injury, affecting drug metabolism

sections.p: Severe autonomic instability, seizures, delirium tremens, hypoglycemia, and electrolyte imbalance can be fatal if untreated.

t.b: Low glucose can mimic or worsen delirium; treat promptly

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and give benzodiazepines titrated to CIWA‑Ar. Avoid antipsychotics alone; use lorazepam or diazepam.

t.b: Diazepam is long‑acting; lorazepam is preferred in hepatic impairment

sections.p: After acute phase, assess for relapse risk, offer counseling, and consider maintenance therapy with baclofen or acamprosate if available.

t.b: Reassess withdrawal severity and plan long‑term management

sections.p: Seizure disorders, anxiety disorders, hyperthyroidism, and acute psychosis can mimic withdrawal.

faq.q: Can alcohol withdrawal happen after a single drink?
faq.a: No, it requires chronic heavy use and abrupt reduction.
Only those with moderate to severe symptoms; mild cases can be monitored.

faq.q: What if a patient has liver disease?
faq.a: Use lorazepam, which is not hepatically metabolised, to avoid accumulation.
